UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                      BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                      )
MS Solar 4, LLC                                       )            Docket No.             ER26-3186-001
                                                      )

                               REQUEST FOR REHEARING AND
                         FOR EXPEDITED ACTION OF MS SOLAR 4, LLC

        Pursuant to section 313(a) of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) 1 and Rule 713 of the

Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 2 MS Solar 4, LLC (“Covington”) 3 respectfully

requests that the Commission expeditiously grant rehearing of its order denying waiver of the

Commercial Operation Date (“COD”) deadline for Covington’s MS Solar 4 Project (“Project”)

and grant an extension of the COD deadline under Covington’s Generator Interconnection

Agreement (“GIA”) as discussed below. 4 The Commission’s denial runs afoul of the

Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”), and with the COD deadline having expired on

September 30, 2026, the GIA for the Project—in which Covington has invested over $60 million—

could terminate before Covington has any meaningful opportunity for Commission or judicial

review absent prompt action in this proceeding.

        The Order violates the APA in two independent respects. First, without acknowledgment

or explanation, the Order departed from longstanding Commission precedent governing the “good

faith” prong of its waiver standard. The Commission has repeatedly found good faith where a

equipment have been secured; a commercial agreement with an offtaker has been reached; project

design is sufficiently complete; and Covington has awarded the Project to an engineering,

procurement, and construction (“EPC”) contractor that is ready to commence work. The Project

also enjoys local support, as evidenced by the tax abatement the local community has granted it. 6

        The Commission nonetheless determined that Covington did not act in good faith because

Covington “should have” anticipated that site conditions would be worse than industry-standard

studies showed and built time into its schedule to address them. 7 That test finds no support in

Commission precedent. To the contrary, the Commission repeatedly has granted waivers to

applicants that demonstrated far less commitment to, and investment in, their projects than

Covington has shown here, including where it was undisputed that the applicant’s own actions

contributed to the delay.

        Second, even on the Order’s own terms, the Commission’s findings that Covington should

have identified the site conditions or cleared the site sooner, and that there was an “unexplained

gap” in Covington’s development, are not the product of reasoned decision-making and run

        Further, in granting rehearing, the Commission should find that the 2026 Waiver Request

satisfies the other three prongs of the Commission’s four-part test for granting tariff waivers. 11

The record amply demonstrates that Covington’s request is limited in scope 12 and that granting

the imminent prospect of termination of its GIA. Termination would eliminate a new, late-stage

solar generation and battery storage resource 15 being developed to offset large load customer

I.      ARGUMENT

        A.         The Order Applies A New And Unworkable Hindsight Test To Find That
                   Covington Did Not Act In Good Faith
        Under the APA, an agency must “provide[] a reasoned explanation for departing from

precedent or treating similar situations differently,” 16 and, when it treats one party differently from

others, “point to a relevant distinction between the two cases.” 17 Relatedly, “the requirement that

an agency provide reasoned explanation for its action would ordinarily demand that it display

awareness that it is changing position.” 18

        The Order contravenes those basic principles. It finds that Covington “should have”

incorporated development risks into the Project’s schedule or been aware of the issue at the time

of its Initial Waiver Request in 2024, and on that basis concludes that “the delays were the result

of Covington’s own inaction, not conditions beyond Covington’s control.” 19 But the Commission

has not previously judged good faith by what a developer should have anticipated in hindsight,

and the Order neither acknowledges nor explains that change. Nor has the Commission deemed a

delay within the control of the developer because it theoretically could have learned of a risk earlier

by taking exceptional measures. That unexplained departure is arbitrary and capricious under the

APA.

Pipeline Co. v. FERC, 71 F.3d 897, 901 (D.C. Cir. 1995)); see also Am. Whitewater v. FERC, 183 F.4th 805, 809
(D.C. Cir. 2026) (“Am. Whitewater”) (agencies must “treat similarly situated parties similarly”).

                      1.      The Order Departs, Without Explanation, From the Commission’s
                             Consistent Application Of The Good Faith Standard
                             a.      The Commission’s “Good Faith” Standard Focuses On A
                                     Showing Of Diligence
           Historically, in determining good faith, the Commission has asked whether the developer

diligently pursued development of the project as a whole and acted promptly once an impediment

became known and actionable. 20 In case after case, the Commission has granted waivers to

developers when they provided evidence that they had invested significant resources into their

projects, met their financial obligations under their GIAs, and continued to take steps to advance

their projects after encountering delays, even where the events necessitating waiver were

foreseeable, avoidable, or caused in part by the developers. 21 In contrast, the Commission denies

waiver for lack of good faith where the applicant fails to provide any evidence showing that it has

made diligent efforts to develop the project, including taking corrective steps when it realized that

it could not timely meet its obligations. 22 Measured against the Commission’s precedent,

Covington clearly meets the good faith prong.

           First, Covington has diligently pursued development of the Project as a whole. When the

Commission granted Covington’s Initial Waiver Request in 2024, the Commission observed that

including investing an additional $32 million in the Project since filing the Initial Waiver

       Second, Covington acted promptly and took corrective action once the full extent of the

site’s challenging topography and hydrology conditions became clear. It revised the Project’s civil

design, which required additional mass grading and retention basins to prevent long-term flooding

1,200 acres, installed more than 30 retention basins, and performed ongoing erosion control and

site maintenance, at an unanticipated cost of more than $7 million (for a total cost of

$12.6 million). 26 Covington also advanced the Project to a financeable, updated Issued-for-

Construction design. 27 When its prior EPC contractor could not accommodate the revised

schedule, Covington re-bid the EPC work and awarded it to Conductor Power. 28 Covington then

executed an agreement with Conductor Power for design and engineering updates, and Conductor

       Covington’s record stands in stark contrast to Oxbow Solar, the only case, to Covington’s

knowledge, where the Commission has denied a request for an extension of a commercial

operation deadline based on a lack of good faith. 30 In Oxbow Solar, the developer issued its

authorization to proceed under its interconnection agreement two and a half years late, and only

after receiving a notice of breach; it had spent only roughly $3 million on the project; and no

interconnection work had begun. 31 Southwest Power Pool, Inc. even noted that the developer had

missed “opportunities” to move the project forward. 32 On that record, the Commission attributed

the delay not to any outside impediment but to the developer’s “own inaction.” 33 Here, by contrast,

Covington has invested over $60 million in the Project, funded network upgrades and

interconnection facilities that are now complete, secured the necessary permits, and achieved

numerous other milestones, including entering exclusivity with a new offtaker and securing

approval to add battery storage through the surplus interconnection process. 34 Under the

Commission’s established standard, that record amply demonstrates good faith.

                           b.       The Good Faith Standard Accommodates Delays Resulting
                                    From Purposeful Changes And Known Risks
       To Covington’s knowledge, the Commission has not found a lack of good faith merely

because a party can identify, in hindsight, some alternative course the developer theoretically could

a delay to be within the control of a developer merely because a risk could have been identified

through exceptional measures. The Commission’s precedent bears this out across a range of

circumstances, including where the risks necessitating waiver were known at the time of an earlier

waiver request, where the full extent of a site risk was only confirmed later in development, and

where the developer’s own decisions affected the project timeline and contributed to the need for

waiver.

          The Commission has granted second waiver requests even where the risks necessitating

waiver were known at the time of the initial waiver request. For example, in Mustang Mile, when

the developer sought its first waiver, it had been litigating its local permit for nearly four years and

precedent, the Commission rested that finding on the “significant resources and effort” expended,

the approximately $50 million invested, and the developer’s steps “to resolve the local permitting

challenges through the state permitting process.” 38 Indeed, even though the developer had flagged

        Similarly, in Shenandoah Hills, the Commission granted a second waiver request to

address delays caused by permit litigation, even though opponents had already challenged the

developer’s county permits when it sought its first waiver. 40 The Commission found good faith to

grant the second waiver because, despite “permit challenges and related litigation,” the developer

the contrary, in finding the waiver limited in scope, the Commission treated the later revocation

and continued litigation as new circumstances that “could not be anticipated.” 42 There is no

principled basis for granting waiver in Mustang Mile and Shenandoah Hills but denying waiver to

Covington. Covington has invested more than the developer in either case and, unlike those

developers, was unaware of the conditions necessitating waiver when it sought its first waiver.

        The Commission has also found good faith where the full extent of a site risk was

confirmed later in development. In IL Solar 1, the Commission granted an extension of the

commercial operation deadline to address delays caused in part by subsidence risk at the project

site. The site had a history of surface and subsurface coal mining, but geotechnical studies

revealing the resulting subsidence risk were not conducted until 2022 and 2023, approximately

       Ratts 2 Solar follows a similar pattern. 45 There, the Commission granted waiver to allow

an extension of the commercial operation deadline to address delays caused by federal wetlands

even more compelling: it relied on a series of standard-industry surveys and studies which failed

to disclose the extent of the site conditions, and, like the developers in IL Solar 1 and Ratts 2 Solar,

        Lastly, the Commission has found good faith and granted waiver where the record

demonstrated that the developer’s own actions had affected the project timeline and contributed to

the need for an extension. In Rose Energy Center, the Commission granted waiver to allow an

and its “full site control.” 53

       In every case discussed in this section, the Commission did not dwell on what the developer

“should have” done or require that the developer’s schedule anticipate every conceivable risk. It

asked instead whether the developer diligently advanced the project as a whole and responded to

obstacles as they arose, and where that showing was made, it found good faith, even where the

developer’s own choices or the timing of its actions contributed to the need for waiver.

       Although the Commission has sometimes noted that delays were beyond the developer’s

control, it has not treated a delay as within the developer’s control merely because the developer

knew of a risk or theoretically could have identified it at an earlier stage. The delays at issue in

this case were no more within the control of Covington than the delays in the cases described

above. Indeed, in contrast to the location of the project in Rock Creek Solar or the permitting issues

in Ratts 2 Solar, Covington only could have detected the topography and hydrology conditions at

the site if Covington had acted imprudently by clear-cutting the site. 56

granted to other applicants whose efforts and commitment to their projects were no greater, and,

in some cases, significantly less, than Covington’s. Such disparate treatment is arbitrary,

capricious, and contrary to law.

                  2.       The Order Distinguishes Precedent On An “Unexplained Gap”—A
                           Factor That Was Not A Basis For The Commission’s Prior Good Faith
                           Findings
       The Order also errs in distinguishing Ratts 2 Solar, Clover Creek, and IL Solar 1, which

Covington cited as precedent where the Commission granted waiver because unforeseen

circumstances delayed the relevant projects. 57 The Order set those cases aside on the ground that

in each case “there was no unexplained gap in time during which the applicant was not diligently

assessing land conditions,” which the Order found “not . . . to be true in the case with Covington.” 58

That attempt falls short. An agency that treats one party differently from others “must . . . point to

a relevant distinction between the two cases.” 59

       Whether there was an “unexplained gap” in assessing land conditions is not a relevant

distinction, because the Commission did not rely on any such gap analysis in those cases or any

other cases to Covington’s knowledge. Instead, the Commission found good faith based on the

developer’s overall progress on the project. In each of these cases, the Commission looked to

whether the developer continued to advance the project as a whole. In Clover Creek, the

Commission found good faith because the developer had expended significant funds and

“diligently worked towards meeting” its milestones, securing land rights and permits, and

procurement in finding that the developer “worked diligently to fully address” the known

reliance on a distinction that played no role in those decisions is arbitrary and capricious.

                   3.       The Order’s Hindsight Standard Is Inconsistent With The Limited-
                            Scope And Concrete-Problem Prongs Of The Waiver Standard
        The Order’s hindsight standard creates a conflict between the good faith requirement, on

the one hand, and the limited-scope and concrete-problem requirements, on the other, and thus

puts developers in an impossible position that cannot be reconciled with Commission precedent. 63

II.    STATEMENT OF ISSUES AND SPECIFICATION OF ERRORS

       Pursuant to Rule 713(c) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 96 Covington

sets forth the following issues and specifies the following errors found in the Order:

       A.         The Commission erred in applying a new and unworkable hindsight test to find that
                  Covington did not act in good faith, on the ground that Covington “should have”
                  anticipated the site conditions and built time into its schedule to address them.

                  1.       The Commission erred by departing, without explanation, from its
                           consistent application of the good faith prong of its four-part test for
                           granting tariff waivers. The Commission has found good faith where a
                           developer diligently advanced its project as a whole and took corrective
                           action once an impediment became known and actionable, even where the
                           circumstances necessitating waiver were foreseeable to, or caused by the
                           actions of, the developer. The Commission has denied waivers for lack of
                           good faith only where the developer failed to show any such diligent efforts.
                           The Commission’s failure to find that Covington satisfied the good faith
                           standard or to acknowledge or explain its departure from that precedent is
                           arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); West
                           Deptford, 766 F.3d at 20 (quoting ANR Pipeline Co. v. FERC, 71 F.3d at
                           901) (“It is textbook administrative law that an agency must ‘provide[] a
                           reasoned explanation for departing from precedent or treating similar
                           situations differently[.]’”); FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S.
                           at 515 (holding that an agency must “display awareness that it is changing
                           position” and “show that there are good reasons for the new policy”); N.C.
                           Utils. Comm’n v. FERC, 42 F.3d at 666 (rejecting FERC order where FERC
                           failed to “sufficiently explain[] its departure from prior cases[]”); Am.
                           Whitewater, 183 F.4th at 809 (agencies must “treat similarly situated parties
                           similarly”); id. at 812 (quoting West Deptford, 766 F.3d at 17) (“The
                           Commission, however, ‘cannot depart from [its] rulings without provid[ing]
                           a reasoned analysis indicating that prior policies and standards are being
                           deliberately changed.’”). See also Rosner Dissent at PP 6-7 (describing
                           existing precedent on good faith).

                  2.       The Commission erred by distinguishing Ratts 2 Solar, Clover Creek, and
                           IL Solar 1 on the basis of an “unexplained gap” in assessing land conditions,
                           a factor that was not the basis for the Commission’s good faith findings in
                           those cases. Because the Commission must “point to a relevant distinction
